title: Local SEO & Google Business Profile
subtitle: Get found by nearby customers: profile optimisation, reviews, citations, local pages, AI-era visibility and tracking
description:
When people search "dentist near me", "AC repair Dubai" or "best karahi in Lahore" — or ask an AI assistant the same question — the businesses that appear win calls, visits and bookings. This practical course shows business owners, marketers and agency staff how local search really works in 2026 and how to compete within Google's rules.

You will learn Google's stated local factors (relevance, distance and prominence), how AI Overviews, AI Mode and Maps' AI features use your information, and how to set up, verify and protect a Google Business Profile. You will score a profile with a hands-on checklist, run a policy-compliant review system (including the latest rules on incentives, staff names and kiosks), turn reviews into insights, fix citations, build local pages that are not doorways, earn local links, and handle suspensions and competitor spam.

Finally, you will measure with grid tracking, Search Console, Business Profile data, GA4, Python and Sheets, and run a full audit with a 90-day plan. Examples come from the UK, US, UAE, KSA and Pakistan.

lessons.title: How local search works
lessons.body:
### What "local search" means

Local search covers any query where the searcher wants something nearby or in a specific place: "dentist near me", "best biryani in Karachi", "AC repair Dubai Marina", "plumber Manchester". Google shows several local features:

- **The local pack (map pack)**: a map with a small set of business listings, usually near the top of results.
- **The local finder**: the expanded list you see after clicking "More places".
- **Google Maps results**: searches made directly in Maps.
- **Organic results** with local intent: city service pages, directories, review sites.
- **AI features** in Search and Maps — AI Overviews and AI Mode answers that recommend places, and Gemini-powered "ask about this place" features in Maps that summarise reviews and profile details. They are evolving quickly; the next lesson covers them, and the fundamentals in this course still underpin them.

Most local businesses need visibility in **both** the map results (driven largely by Google Business Profile) and organic results (driven by the website).

### The three local ranking factors Google documents

Google's own help documentation says local results are based mainly on:

1. **Relevance** — how well a Business Profile matches what someone is searching for. Influenced by categories, business description, services, products, reviews content and your website.
2. **Distance** — how far each potential result is from the location used in the search (the searcher's location or a location named in the query).
3. **Prominence** — how well known the business is. Google mentions information from across the web (links, articles, directories), review count and ratings, and your position in web results.

Google also states that you **cannot pay** to improve your Business Profile's local ranking, and that there is no way to request or pay for a better position.

### What you can and cannot control

| Factor | Control | Levers |
|---|---|---|
| Relevance | High | Correct categories, complete profile, services, clear website content |
| Distance | Very low | Your real address; you cannot fake proximity (virtual offices violate guidelines) |
| Prominence | Medium, over time | Reviews, local links and coverage, citations, organic strength |

Understanding distance is liberating: a business will naturally rank better near its location and worse far away. That is not a failure of your SEO — it's how local search works. For wider coverage, you use organic pages and, where legitimate, additional real locations.

### Organic local results matter too

Many valuable queries show organic results beneath or instead of the pack — especially research-heavy services ("cost of invisalign London", "how to choose a wedding photographer in Lahore"). Your website's service pages, location pages, content and links influence these. Google also lists "your position in web results" as part of prominence, so organic and local SEO reinforce each other.

### How people search locally

- **Explicit location**: "tailor in Gulberg Lahore".
- **Implicit location**: "tailor" — Google infers local intent and uses the device's location.
- **"Near me"**: Google uses the device's location; you do not need to stuff "near me" into your content.
- **Branded**: "[business name] opening hours" — your profile must be accurate.
- **Discovery in Maps**: people browsing categories on the map.

### Worked example

A family-owned bakery in Jumeirah, Dubai, wonders why it ranks in the pack for "bakery" when searched near its shop but not from Dubai Marina. That is distance. To reach more customers across the city, it:

1. Perfects its Business Profile for relevance (primary category "Bakery", secondary "Cake shop"; products for custom cakes).
2. Builds prominence with steady reviews, local press about its Emirati date cakes, and listings in reputable local directories.
3. Creates website content for delivery across Dubai and a custom cake ordering page that can rank organically citywide.

### Common myths

- "Keyword stuffing the business name is a ranking hack." It violates Google's guidelines and can lead to suspension.
- "Paying for Google Ads improves map rankings." Google says it does not.
- "A virtual office will make us rank in a new city." Addresses must be where you actually serve customers in person or are staffed; virtual offices typically violate guidelines.
- "Posting daily guarantees top rankings." Activity helps engagement, not guaranteed positions.

### How to read Google's three factors in practice

Google's help page on improving local ranking describes the factors in plain language: **relevance** is how well a profile matches what someone searched for; **distance** is how far each result is from the location used in the search (or, if the searcher doesn't specify one, what Google knows about their location); **prominence** is how well known a business is, informed by information from across the web such as links, articles and directories, plus review count and ratings. It also notes that a business's position in web results counts towards prominence.

Turn that into a working diagnosis whenever a client asks "why aren't we in the pack?":

| Symptom | Likely factor | First checks |
|---|---|---|
| Visible next door, invisible 2 km away | Distance (normal) + weak prominence | Grid tracking; reviews vs competitors; local links |
| Not visible even next door | Relevance or eligibility | Primary category; profile completeness; suspension or duplicates |
| Visible for brand, not for services | Relevance | Services, categories, website service pages |
| Visible in Maps, not in organic | Website weakness | Service and location pages; technical SEO |

### Hands-on: search like your customers

1. Open a private browser window, sign out, and set the search location (or use a location-simulation feature in a local rank-tracking tool such as BrightLocal or a similar geo-grid tracker).
2. Search your three most valuable service queries with and without a city name, plus one "near me" query.
3. Record for each: whether a local pack appears, who is in it, whether an AI Overview appears and which businesses or sources it mentions, and which directories rank organically.
4. Repeat from two other points in your catchment.

```text
Query | Location point | Pack? | Pack businesses | AI answer? | Sources/businesses named | Top organic directories
```

This 20-minute table is the start of every local audit in this course.

### Common mistakes

- Measuring local rankings only from the office computer (which is right next to the business).
- Ignoring organic local results.
- Treating the Business Profile as "set and forget".

lessons.title: Local search in the AI era: AI Overviews, AI Mode and Maps
lessons.body:
### What searchers see now

Local discovery used to be "map pack plus ten blue links". In 2026 a searcher may also see:

- **AI Overviews** in Search for questions such as "best family dentist in Jumeirah for nervous kids" — a generated summary that can name businesses and link to sources, sometimes alongside a local pack.
- **AI Mode** in Search — a conversational experience where people ask follow-ups ("which of these are open late on Friday?") and get answers that draw on Business Profile data, reviews and the web.
- **Gemini-powered features in Google Maps** — people can ask about a place ("is there parking?", "is it good for groups?") and get answers summarised from the profile, reviews, photos and other information. In many markets this has replaced the old public Questions & Answers section.
- **Review summaries and highlights** generated from customer reviews.

Google's guidance for generative AI features in Search (May 2026) is that they run on the same foundations as Search: there is no separate "AI local ranking" to game. For local businesses, the practical inputs are the same ones this course teaches — accurate, complete Business Profile data; genuine reviews that describe real experiences; a website that states facts clearly; and consistent information across reputable sources.

### What AI answers draw on (and what you control)

| Source | Examples | Your lever |
|---|---|---|
| Business Profile data | Categories, services, attributes, hours, menu, products | Complete and accurate; update special hours |
| Reviews and photos | What customers mention; visual evidence | Steady, compliant review flow; real photos |
| Your website | Service pages, FAQs, prices, policies | Clear facts in text (not only in images or PDFs) |
| Third-party sources | Directories, local media, review sites, forums, videos | Citations, local PR, community presence |

### Make your facts "answerable"

AI answers work best with explicit facts. If customers often ask "do you have parking?", "do you treat children?", "do you speak Arabic/Urdu?", "is there a female doctor?", make sure the answer exists in **several places**: an attribute on the profile (where one exists), a line in the relevant service description, an FAQ on the website and — naturally — in reviews from customers who experienced it. Never write fake reviews or seed questions to plant answers; that breaches Google's fake engagement policies.

### Hands-on: an "AI questions" audit

1. List 15 questions customers ask before choosing you (from calls, WhatsApp, front desk, reviews).
2. For each, check where the answer currently appears: profile field/attribute, website text, reviews, third-party listings.
3. Ask the same questions in Google (AI Mode where available), in Google Maps' ask feature on your own profile, and in one other assistant.
4. Record whether the answer is correct, missing or wrong, and fix the source.

```text
Question | Profile? | Website? | Reviews mention? | AI answer (date, surface) | Correct? | Fix
Is there parking? | attribute yes | FAQ no | 3 reviews | Maps: "street parking only" (wrong) | ✗ | add FAQ + parking photos
```

### Managing the profile with AI

In 2026 Google began rolling out the option to **connect a Business Profile to Gemini**, letting owners update information, draft review replies and read performance data by chatting (availability varies by country and account type; some features were not launched in the UK and EEA at first). Treat AI-drafted changes like any other edit: check the facts, keep the tone human, and never let an assistant publish claims you cannot support.

### Measuring AI-era local visibility

- **Business Profile performance**: calls, direction requests, website clicks, bookings — the outcomes still matter most.
- **Search Console**: impressions and clicks for location and service pages (AI feature traffic is included in Web search totals; the Generative AI performance report adds AI feature impressions by page).
- **GA4**: sessions from the UTM-tagged profile link and from AI assistants' referrals.
- **Your AI questions audit**, repeated quarterly.

### Worked example (illustrative)

A family dental clinic in Jumeirah hears patients say "Google told me you don't treat kids". The audit shows the website mentions children only in an image banner, the profile has no children's service listed, and several reviews describe adult treatments. The clinic adds a "Children's dentistry" service with a short description, a website page with clear text on ages treated and what to expect, photos of the children's treatment room, and starts asking parents (all patients, no gating) for honest reviews. The next quarterly audit shows the answer corrected in Maps and in AI Mode.

### Common mistakes

- Chasing "AI local ranking hacks" instead of fixing facts at the source.
- Putting key facts only in images, PDFs or social posts.
- Planting fake reviews or questions to steer AI answers.
- Letting an AI assistant change profile details without human checks.
keyTakeaways: AI Overviews, AI Mode and Gemini features in Maps draw on Business Profile data, reviews, your website and third-party sources.
There is no separate AI local ranking to game; accurate data and genuine reviews are the inputs.
Make common customer questions answerable in several places: profile fields, website text and real reviews.
Audit AI answers quarterly and fix wrong facts at their source; check AI-drafted profile edits before publishing.

lessons.title: Setting up and verifying your Google Business Profile
lessons.body:
### Who is eligible

A Google Business Profile (GBP) is for businesses that make **in-person contact with customers** during stated hours:

- **Storefront businesses** — customers visit you (shops, restaurants, clinics, salons).
- **Service-area businesses (SABs)** — you visit customers (plumbers, cleaners, mobile car wash, home tutors).
- **Hybrid** — both (a café that caters; a repair shop that also does call-outs).

Online-only businesses without in-person contact are generally not eligible. Rented or virtual offices, mailboxes and co-working addresses where you are not staffed during business hours typically violate guidelines.

### The guidelines that matter most at setup

Google's guidelines for representing your business are strict. The big ones:

**Business name** — use your real-world name as it appears consistently on your signage, stationery and branding. Do **not** add keywords, locations or taglines.

```text
Correct:   Al Noor Dental Clinic
Violation: Al Noor Dental Clinic - Best Dentist Dubai | Teeth Whitening | Braces
```

**Address** — a precise, real address. SABs should **hide** their address and list service areas instead. One profile per location.

**Phone** — a local number that reaches the business directly where possible (call-tracking numbers are acceptable if configured properly, with the main number as an additional phone).

**Website** — link to the most relevant page; for multi-location businesses, the specific location page.

**Hours** — accurate regular hours; special hours for holidays (Eid, Ramadan timings, Christmas, bank holidays).

### Step-by-step setup

1. **Search Google Maps first** for your business name and address. A profile may already exist (created by Google or a customer). If so, claim it instead of creating a duplicate; if someone else owns it, use Google's request-access process.
2. **Create or claim** at the Business Profile manager with a business Google account that the organisation controls (not a freelancer's personal account).
3. **Choose the primary category** (Module 2 covers this in depth).
4. **Enter location or service areas**.
5. **Add contact details**: phone, website.
6. **Verify**. Google chooses which methods are available; they can include **video recording** (showing signage, the location, tools of the trade, proof of management such as keys or business documents), phone or SMS, email, or postcard. Some businesses need to complete more than one step.
7. **Complete the profile**: description, services, products, attributes, photos, hours.

### Verification tips

- Prepare for video verification: a continuous recording showing the street or area, the exterior signage, then inside, plus proof you manage the business (unlocking the door, point-of-sale, business licence). For SABs, show branded vehicles and equipment.
- Make sure the details you submit **match** your real signage and documents. Mismatches trigger rejections.
- Don't make many edits to core details while verification is pending.
- If verification fails repeatedly, use the support routes Google provides rather than creating new profiles.

### Ownership and access management

- **Primary owner**: a business-controlled account (e.g. a shared marketing Google account with multi-factor authentication).
- **Owners and managers**: add agency staff as managers, not primary owners. Remove access when people leave.
- Agencies should never hold the primary ownership of a client's profile. It creates disputes and risk.

### Features that have changed

Google periodically retires and adds GBP features: **chat/messaging** was discontinued in 2024 and **websites built with Business Profile** were shut down the same year. The classic public **Questions & Answers** section has been replaced in many markets by AI-generated answers ("ask about this place" features in Maps powered by Gemini), while owners have been able to keep answering existing questions from the dashboard. In 2026 Google also began rolling out the option to **connect a Business Profile to Gemini** so owners can manage the profile, draft review replies and read performance data in natural language (availability varies by country and account type). Always check current Google Business Profile Help rather than old tutorials.

### Suspensions

Profiles can be suspended for guideline violations (keyword-stuffed names, ineligible addresses, suspicious edits) or sometimes in error. If suspended:

1. Read the notice and review guidelines honestly.
2. Fix any violation (e.g. remove keywords from the name).
3. Submit an appeal with evidence: business licence, utility bill, signage photos, website showing the same details.

### Hands-on: a setup and verification pack

Before you start, prepare a folder so verification succeeds first time:

```text
/gbp-setup
  canonical-nap.txt          exact name, address (or service areas), phone, website URL, hours
  proof-of-business/         trade licence or registration, utility bill, lease (names/addresses match)
  signage-photos/            exterior sign in daylight, street view context, interior
  verification-video-plan.txt
     1. Street or building exterior showing location context (street sign/landmark)
     2. Permanent signage with the business name
     3. Walk inside: reception/workspace, equipment or stock
     4. Proof of management: unlock the door, open the till or show business documents
     SAB: branded vehicle, tools of the trade, business documents
  access.txt                 primary owner account (business-controlled, MFA on), managers list
```

Record the verification in one continuous take, in good light, and make sure every detail you show matches what you entered. Keep the folder: you will need the same evidence if the profile is ever suspended and you have to appeal.

### Common mistakes

- Creating a new profile when one already exists (duplicates).
- Agencies owning client profiles.
- Adding city names to the business name "for SEO".
- Using a co-working or virtual office address.

lessons.title: Categories, services and attributes
lessons.body:
### The primary category is your most important relevance choice

Your **primary category** tells Google what your business fundamentally is. It strongly influences which searches you appear for and which features your profile gets (booking buttons, menus, services lists). Google allows one primary category and additional secondary categories (up to nine additional at the time of writing).

### Choosing categories: a step-by-step method

1. **List your core services** and how customers search for them.
2. **Find the matching categories** in GBP's category list. Categories are fixed — you must choose from Google's list, which differs by language and country.
3. **Research competitors**: check the primary and secondary categories of businesses ranking in the pack for your main queries. (Browser extensions and local SEO tools can reveal categories; you can also see the primary category on the listing.)
4. **Pick the primary category** that matches your main revenue service *and* the query you most want. For a clinic that mainly does orthodontics, "Orthodontist" may be better than "Dentist" — or vice versa, depending on demand and what the clinic mainly is.
5. **Add secondary categories** only for services you genuinely provide as a meaningful part of the business. Irrelevant categories dilute relevance and can be removed by Google.
6. **Test and measure**: category changes can shift visibility. Change one thing at a time and track rankings and actions over several weeks.

Example:

| Business | Primary | Secondary |
|---|---|---|
| Lahore restaurant specialising in Karahi, also does catering | Pakistani restaurant | Caterer, Barbecue restaurant, Takeout restaurant |
| Dubai AC repair company visiting homes | Air conditioning repair service | Air conditioning contractor, HVAC contractor |
| London accountancy firm for small businesses | Accountant | Tax preparation service, Bookkeeping service |

### Business description

750 characters to explain what you do, who you serve and what makes you different. Write for people: natural language, key services, areas served, years in business, specialisms. Do not include URLs, promotional claims ("best", "cheapest"), or keyword lists. Google says the description is used for relevance only indirectly; its main job is to help customers choose.

### Services

Add **services** for each category (Google suggests some; you can add custom ones). Include a short description and, where sensible, price or "from" price. Services help relevance and customer understanding.

```text
Service: Emergency boiler repair
Description: Same-day call-outs across South Manchester for gas and combi boilers.
Gas Safe registered engineers. Call-out fee from £65 (illustrative).
```

### Products

Products are useful not just for retailers: service businesses can list packages ("Wedding photography package — full day"). Include a photo, name, description, category, price (optional) and a link to the relevant page.

### Attributes

Attributes describe features: accessibility (wheelchair-accessible entrance), amenities (Wi-Fi, parking), service options (delivery, dine-in, online appointments), payments, and identity-based attributes where available (e.g. women-owned — self-declared and region-dependent). Complete all that accurately apply; they help customers filter and appear in profile details.

### Opening hours and special hours

- Accurate regular hours are important — Google may show "Closed" at the time of search, which affects visibility and clicks for "open now" queries.
- Set **special hours** for public holidays, Ramadan schedules, Eid, Christmas, New Year.
- Use **more hours** for specific services (delivery hours, drive-through, senior hours) where available.

### Keep the profile in sync with the website

Relevance is reinforced when your website says the same things: a page for each main service, the same business name, address and phone, and schema markup (`LocalBusiness` subtype) matching the profile.

```json
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "Dentist",
  "name": "Al Noor Dental Clinic",
  "address": {"@type": "PostalAddress", "streetAddress": "Office 204, Example Tower, Al Wasl Road",
              "addressLocality": "Dubai", "addressCountry": "AE"},
  "telephone": "+971-4-000-0000",
  "url": "https://www.alnoordental.example/",
  "openingHoursSpecification": [{"@type": "OpeningHoursSpecification",
    "dayOfWeek": ["Monday","Tuesday","Wednesday","Thursday","Saturday","Sunday"],
    "opens": "09:00", "closes": "21:00"}]
}
```

### Hands-on: category research sheet

Research categories systematically for your top three queries:

```text
Query | Competitor | Rank in pack | Primary category | Secondary categories (if visible) | Notes
```

Collect the primary category from each competitor's listing (it is shown on the profile) and use a local SEO browser extension or tool to see secondary categories. Then count which primary category appears most among the top results for each query:

```text
=QUERY(A2:F100, "select D, count(B) where A = 'dentist' group by D order by count(B) desc", 1)
```

A category that dominates the top results is strong evidence of what Google associates with that query — but only choose it if it truly describes your core business.

### Service descriptions that help people and relevance

Write each service as: **what it is + who it's for + a distinctive detail + price guidance where sensible**, 1–3 sentences, no keyword lists. Keep services consistent with the matching page on your website so the two reinforce each other. If you connect your profile to Gemini, you can ask it to draft service descriptions from your website — then edit for accuracy and remove any claims you cannot back up (Google's policies prohibit misleading content).

### Common mistakes

- Choosing a broad primary category ("Store") when a specific one exists.
- Adding many loosely related secondary categories.
- Keyword-stuffed descriptions.
- Forgetting holiday hours, leading to angry reviews from customers who find the shop closed.
keyTakeaways: The primary category is the most important relevance choice; pick from Google's list based on core revenue and demand.
Add secondary categories only for genuine, meaningful services; test changes one at a time.
Complete services, products and attributes accurately; write a helpful, non-promotional description.
Keep regular and special hours accurate and the website consistent with the profile.

lessons.title: Photos, posts and ongoing profile management
lessons.body:
### A Business Profile is a living asset

Profiles that are complete, accurate and active tend to convert more searchers into customers. Google also notes that complete and accurate information helps match profiles to searches. This lesson turns profile maintenance into a simple routine.

### Photos and videos

Photos help people choose. Upload real, high-quality images:

| Type | What to show |
|---|---|
| Logo and cover | Brand recognition; cover photo representing the business |
| Exterior | How to recognise the entrance from the street, at different times of day |
| Interior | Atmosphere, cleanliness, seating, waiting area |
| Products/work | Dishes, finished projects, before/after (where appropriate and permitted) |
| Team | Real staff at work (with consent) |
| Short videos | Walk-through, process, a quick introduction |

Tips: use natural light, avoid heavy filters and stock photos, keep images current, and add new photos regularly (for example monthly). Customer photos appear too; report inappropriate ones.

### Posts (updates, offers, events)

GBP posts let you share news, offers and events directly on the profile. They are useful for conversions and freshness of information; treat any ranking effect as unproven.

- **Updates**: new services, seasonal messages, tips.
- **Offers**: with dates and terms; comply with advertising standards and consumer law.
- **Events**: workshops, launches, open days.

Good post structure: an image, a short clear message, a call to action button, and a UTM-tagged link so you can track clicks in analytics.

```text
Ramadan hours & iftar platters
From 1 March we're open 11:00–02:00. Pre-order family iftar platters (serves 6)
by 3pm for same-day pickup. [Order online]
Link: https://www.example.com/iftar?utm_source=google&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=gbp-post
```

### Tracking GBP traffic properly

Add UTM parameters to the **website link** on your profile so GBP visits are distinguishable from other organic traffic:

```text
https://www.example.com/?utm_source=google&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=gbp-listing
```

For multi-location businesses, point each profile to its location page with its own UTM campaign or content value. (Keep the canonical tag on the landing page pointing to the clean URL.)

### Performance insights

The Business Profile **Performance** view shows interactions such as calls, messages where available, bookings, direction requests and website clicks, plus how people found you (searches used, Search vs Maps, mobile vs desktop). Use it for trends, recognising that it is aggregated and sometimes thresholded. Combine it with:

- Call tracking (configured correctly) for phone-heavy businesses.
- Analytics (UTM-tagged visits and conversions).
- Point-of-sale or CRM data asking "how did you hear about us?".

### Handling edits by Google and the public

Anyone can **suggest edits** to a profile, and Google can update information from other sources. Check the profile regularly for changes to hours, categories, address or website that you did not make. The dashboard notifies you of some updates; review and reject incorrect changes promptly.

### Monthly profile routine

```text
Week 1: Check core info (name, address, phone, website, hours, categories) for unwanted edits
        Upload 3–5 new photos
Week 2: Publish a post (update or offer) with UTM link
        Review services/products for accuracy and pricing
Week 3: Respond to all new reviews (see Module 3)
        Check photos added by customers
Week 4: Review Performance insights and analytics; note changes in searches and actions
        Plan next month's posts around calendar moments
```

### Messaging and bookings

Booking buttons can be enabled through supported scheduling partners in some categories and countries. Direct GBP chat was discontinued in 2024, so make sure your phone number and website contact routes work well, and consider WhatsApp links on your website where customers in the Gulf and Pakistan prefer them.

### Spam and competitor violations

If competitors use keyword-stuffed names, fake addresses or fake reviews, you can suggest edits or report them via Google's redressal process with evidence. Do this factually; it can level the playing field, but focus most effort on your own profile.

### Hands-on: a UTM builder in Google Sheets

Keep every profile link consistent with a small builder tab:

```text
A Base URL | B Source | C Medium | D Campaign | E Content (optional) | F Final URL
F2: =A2 & IF(REGEXMATCH(A2, "\?"), "&", "?") &
      "utm_source=" & ENCODEURL(B2) & "&utm_medium=" & ENCODEURL(C2) &
      "&utm_campaign=" & ENCODEURL(D2) & IF(E2<>"", "&utm_content=" & ENCODEURL(E2), "")
```

Use one convention across all locations, for example `utm_source=google`, `utm_medium=organic`, `utm_campaign=gbp-listing` for the website button and `gbp-post` for posts, with `utm_content` set to the location or post name. In GA4, filter sessions where *session campaign* is `gbp-listing` to see profile traffic and its conversions.

### Keep an eye on "collected" and suggested information

Google can update profile details from other sources, public suggestions and — increasingly — information gathered in AI-assisted interactions. In 2026 Google began showing owners a **Collected info** area in some dashboards listing details gathered from recent customer calls or chats, which owners can review and delete if inaccurate. Wherever such controls exist in your account, add them to the monthly routine alongside checking for unwanted edits.

### Posts in practice

Posts support conversions and freshness of information, not guaranteed rankings. Keep them policy-compliant: Google's photos, videos and posts content policy prohibits things like misleading offers, prohibited products and low-quality or irrelevant images, and posts can be removed. Plan them around real calendar moments (Ramadan and Eid, back-to-school, national days, seasonal services) and always include a UTM-tagged link.

### Common mistakes

- Using stock photos or overly edited images.
- Posting without tracking, so nobody knows what works.
- Ignoring public edits until hours or phone numbers are wrong.
- Relying only on GBP insights without connecting to real business outcomes.

lessons.title: Hands-on: the GBP optimisation checklist and scoring sheet
lessons.body:
### Why a scored checklist

"Optimise the profile" is too vague to delegate or measure. A scored checklist turns it into specific, checkable items with evidence, so a junior team member, a franchisee or a client can run it and you can compare locations over time.

### The checklist (score 0 = missing/wrong, 1 = partial, 2 = complete and accurate)

**A. Eligibility and ownership (fix first — risk items)**

| # | Item | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| A1 | Business is eligible (in-person contact; real, staffed address or SAB with hidden address) | Signage photo, lease |
| A2 | Primary owner is a business-controlled account with MFA; agency/staff are managers | Users list screenshot |
| A3 | No duplicate profiles for the same location | Maps search for name/phone |
| A4 | Name matches real-world signage exactly (no keywords/locations/taglines) | Signage photo |

**B. Core information**

| # | Item |
|---|---|
| B1 | Primary category is the most specific accurate category for core revenue |
| B2 | Secondary categories are genuine services only |
| B3 | Address accurate (or hidden with realistic service areas for SABs) |
| B4 | Phone reaches the business; call-tracking set up as primary with main number as additional (if used) |
| B5 | Website link goes to the right page (location page for multi-location) with UTM tags |
| B6 | Regular hours accurate; special hours set for the next holidays (Ramadan, Eid, national days, Christmas) |
| B7 | Description helpful, specific, no URLs or promotional superlatives |

**C. Depth**

| # | Item |
|---|---|
| C1 | Services listed for every core service, with 1–3 sentence descriptions |
| C2 | Products/packages with photos, descriptions and links where relevant |
| C3 | All accurate attributes completed (accessibility, amenities, payments, service options) |
| C4 | Booking, menu or ordering links set up where the category supports them |
| C5 | Frequent customer questions answered in profile fields and on the website |

**D. Visual and activity**

| # | Item |
|---|---|
| D1 | Logo and cover photo set |
| D2 | Exterior photos help people find the entrance; interior, team and work photos are real and recent (last 90 days) |
| D3 | At least one post in the last 30 days with a UTM-tagged link |
| D4 | No inappropriate or outdated customer photos left unreported |

**E. Reviews (see Module 3)**

| # | Item |
|---|---|
| E1 | Compliant review request process live (all customers, no incentives, no gating, no staff-name requests) |
| E2 | Every review in the last 90 days has a response |
| E3 | Review velocity and rating benchmarked against top 3 competitors |

**F. Monitoring**

| # | Item |
|---|---|
| F1 | Unwanted edits checked in the last 30 days (including any "collected info" area) |
| F2 | Performance data reviewed monthly alongside GA4 and call data |

### Build the scoring sheet

Put item IDs in column A, descriptions in B, scores (0–2) in C, evidence links in D and owner/date in E. Then:

```text
Section score (e.g. B):  =SUMIF(A:A, "B*", C:C) / (COUNTIF(A:A, "B*") * 2)
Overall score:           =SUM(C2:C40) / (COUNTA(A2:A40) * 2)
Risk alert:              =IF(COUNTIFS(A:A, "A*", C:C, "<2")>0, "FIX ELIGIBILITY/OWNERSHIP FIRST", "")
```

Format the section scores as percentages and add conditional formatting (red < 50%, amber 50–79%, green ≥ 80%). For multi-location brands, copy the sheet per location and build a summary tab with `IMPORTRANGE` or a simple copy-paste of each location's section scores.

### A description template

```text
[Business name] is a [primary category in plain words] in [area/city] serving [who].
We offer [3–5 core services in natural language]. [Distinctive fact: years, qualifications,
languages spoken, specialism]. [Practical detail: parking, accessibility, booking method].
```

Example: *"Noor Opticians is an independent optician in Gulberg, Lahore, serving families and professionals since 2009. We offer eye tests, children's eyewear, contact lens fittings and same-day glasses repairs. Our optometrists speak Urdu, Punjabi and English. Free parking is available behind the shop, and appointments can be booked online or by phone."*

### Worked example (illustrative)

A 6-branch pharmacy chain in the UAE runs the sheet across all branches. Section A flags one branch whose profile is owned by a former manager's personal account and another with a duplicate listing. Section B shows three branches missing Eid special hours. Section C shows no services listed anywhere. The team fixes ownership and the duplicate first, then sets holiday hours across all branches in one session, then adds services from a central template with branch-specific details. The summary tab moves from mostly amber to mostly green within a month, and the sheet becomes the monthly QA routine.

### Common mistakes

- Scoring from memory instead of checking the live profile.
- Fixing photos and posts before ownership and eligibility risks.
- Using one generic description for every branch.
- Treating 100% as "done" — the checklist is a monthly routine, not a one-off.
keyTakeaways: A scored checklist makes GBP optimisation specific, delegable and comparable across locations.
Always fix eligibility, ownership, duplicates and name issues before cosmetic improvements.
Use section scores, a risk alert and conditional formatting to prioritise and track progress.
Run the checklist monthly; for multi-location brands, summarise section scores per branch.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does the section formula =SUMIF(A:A, "B*", C:C) / (COUNTIF(A:A, "B*") * 2) calculate?
options: The share of possible points achieved in section B
knowledgeCheck.explanation: It sums the scores of items whose ID starts with B and divides by the maximum possible (2 points per item).

lessons.title: Earning reviews the policy-compliant way
lessons.body:
### Why reviews matter locally

Google lists review count and rating as part of **prominence**, and reviews are often the deciding factor for customers choosing between businesses in the pack. Review content can also reinforce relevance — customers naturally mention services ("my root canal was painless") and locations.

### The rules: Google's review policies

Google's prohibited and restricted content policies for reviews include:

- **Fake engagement**: reviews that do not reflect a genuine experience, reviews written by the business or its staff, reviews bought from third parties.
- **Incentives**: you must not offer or accept money, products, discounts or other benefits in exchange for reviews, or to change or remove reviews.
- **Selective solicitation (review gating)**: you should not discourage negative reviews or selectively ask only satisfied customers for reviews.
- **Conflicts of interest**: owners reviewing their own business, employees reviewing their employer, reviewing competitors.

Google's policies also prohibit merchants from asking staff to solicit reviews that include specific content, **including content that identifies a staff member** ("please mention Sarah in your review"), and Google's guidance has long told businesses not to set up review stations or kiosks at their premises. Google actively removes policy-violating reviews, and its **Business Profile restrictions for policy violations** can include temporarily blocking a profile from receiving new reviews, unpublishing existing reviews for a period, and showing a warning to customers that fake reviews were removed. Consumer protection laws apply too — for example the US FTC's rule banning fake reviews and testimonials (in force since October 2024, with civil penalties per violation; the FTC sent warning letters to businesses in December 2025) and the UK's Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, whose ban on fake reviews and concealed incentivised reviews applies from April 2025.

### Building a review system (not a one-off campaign)

A sudden burst of reviews followed by silence looks unnatural and does not reflect ongoing service. Aim for a **steady flow**.

**1. Get your review link**
In the Business Profile, use "Ask for reviews" to get a short link or QR code that opens the review form directly.

**2. Identify the moments of delight**
The best time to ask is right after a positive moment:

| Business | Moment |
|---|---|
| Restaurant | When the bill is paid or the customer compliments the food |
| Clinic | After the follow-up confirming the treatment went well |
| Tradesperson | When the job is finished and checked with the customer |
| E-commerce with showroom | After delivery confirmation |
| Agency | After a successful project milestone |

**3. Ask everyone**
Ask all customers, not just the happy ones (no gating). Most customers who had a good experience will be glad to help; those with issues give you a chance to learn.

**4. Make it effortless**
- Short SMS, WhatsApp or email with the direct link.
- QR code on receipts, table cards, invoices, delivery packaging.
- Staff trained to ask verbally in a natural way.

**5. Use neutral language**

```text
Thanks for visiting Noor Opticians today, Hamza. If you have a minute, we'd appreciate
your honest review — it helps us improve and helps others choose: [short link]
```

Avoid: "Please give us 5 stars", "Leave a review for 10% off your next visit".

**6. Follow up once**
A single reminder a few days later is reasonable. Do not pester.

### Multi-language reviews

In the UAE, KSA and Pakistan, customers may review in Arabic, Urdu or English. All are fine. Respond in the language of the review where you can.

### Reviews on other platforms

Depending on industry and market, customers also check other platforms: Tripadvisor (hospitality), Trustpilot, Facebook, industry-specific sites (healthcare directories, wedding directories), and app stores. Balance your requests across platforms that matter to your customers, following each platform's own rules.

### Staff incentives: be careful

Rewarding staff for the **number** of reviews collected can push them into pressuring customers or gating. If you use staff incentives, tie them to service quality and following the process, not to star ratings, and check they don't breach platform policies.

### Measuring review performance

- New reviews per month (velocity) and trend.
- Average rating trend.
- Response rate and response time.
- Themes in review content (what customers praise or complain about).
- Share of customers asked vs reviews received.

### Illustrative example

A physiotherapy clinic in Birmingham adds a review request to its discharge process: the physio mentions it at the last session, and reception sends an SMS with the review link the same day. Over the following months the clinic receives a steady stream of reviews rather than occasional bursts, and review text frequently mentions specific treatments. (Illustrative scenario.)

### Hands-on: a compliant review request kit

```text
1. Review link: Business Profile → "Ask for reviews" → copy short link / download QR code
2. SMS/WhatsApp (send to every customer after service; one reminder after 3–5 days):
   "Thanks for choosing [Business], [Name]. If you have a minute, we'd appreciate your honest
    review — it helps us improve and helps others choose: [link]. Reply STOP to opt out."
3. Email version: same wording + a single button; no star graphics, no "5-star" prompts.
4. Printed QR: receipts, invoices, delivery inserts, table cards — "Tell us how we did".
5. Staff script: "If you have a moment later, an honest review really helps us."
   Never: "Please mention my name", "Leave 5 stars", "Do it now on our tablet".
```

Check local messaging rules before sending (consent for marketing messages, opt-outs, WhatsApp Business policies). Log requests (date, channel, customer ID — not the review content) so you can calculate the ask-to-review rate without storing unnecessary personal data.

### Track velocity in a sheet

```text
A Month | B Reviews received | C Customers served | D Requests sent | E Avg rating
Ask-to-review rate:   =IFERROR(B2/D2, "")
Coverage of asks:     =IFERROR(D2/C2, "")      // are we asking everyone?
3-month velocity:     =AVERAGE(B2:B4)
```

A low "coverage of asks" is a process problem (staff not asking); a low ask-to-review rate is usually a friction or timing problem.

### Common mistakes

- Offering discounts or prize draws for reviews.
- Only sending review links to customers who rated you highly in an internal survey.
- Posting reviews "on behalf of" customers.
- Asking everyone on one day, then never again.

lessons.title: Responding to reviews and dealing with fake ones
lessons.body:
### Why responses matter

Responding to reviews shows prospective customers that you care, turns some unhappy customers around, and demonstrates professionalism. Google encourages businesses to respond to reviews. Responses are public — write for the next hundred readers, not only the reviewer.

### Response principles

1. **Respond to every review**, positive and negative, within a few days (faster for negatives).
2. **Be human and specific**. Mention what they mentioned.
3. **Never reveal private information** (medical details, order contents, addresses). This is especially important in healthcare, legal and financial services — confidentiality rules may apply.
4. **Stay calm**. Never argue publicly.
5. **Take resolution offline** with a direct contact route.
6. **Keep it natural** — do not stuff keywords into responses.

### Templates to adapt (not copy verbatim)

**Positive review**

```text
Thank you, Maria! We're so glad the team could fit your boiler repair in the same day,
and that Tom explained everything clearly. We'll pass on your kind words. — Jake, Owner
```

**Mixed review**

```text
Thanks for the feedback, Adeel. Glad you enjoyed the karahi — and you're right, the wait
on Friday evening was too long. We've added another server for weekend peaks. We hope to
welcome you back soon. — Sana, Manager
```

**Negative review**

```text
Hi Khalid, I'm sorry your installation wasn't completed on the agreed day — that's not the
standard we set. I'd like to understand what happened and make it right. Please call me
directly on 04 000 0000 or email ops@example.com. — Rashid, Operations Manager
```

**Healthcare (privacy-safe)**

```text
Thank you for your feedback. We take all concerns seriously, but to protect patient
privacy we can't discuss details here. Please contact our practice manager on
020 0000 0000 so we can look into this personally.
```

### Turning negatives into improvements

Log negative themes monthly (waiting times, pricing clarity, communication). Fixing root causes improves future reviews more than any response template. When you have genuinely resolved an issue, it's fine to follow up privately and — without pressure or incentives — let the customer know they're welcome to update their review if they wish. Never make any offer conditional on changing or removing a review.

### Identifying fake or policy-violating reviews

Warning signs:

- Reviewer never visited (no record of the name, date or service).
- Profile has reviewed many businesses in distant cities on the same day.
- Content is off-topic, hateful, contains personal attacks or conflicts of interest (e.g. a former employee or a competitor).
- A sudden wave of 1-star reviews with similar wording (review bombing).

### Removing policy-violating reviews

1. **Flag/report the review** through the Business Profile (or Maps), choosing the most accurate policy reason.
2. If it remains, use Google's **review management tool** to check the status of reports and, where available, **appeal** decisions.
3. For extortion attempts (someone demanding payment to remove negative reviews), Google has specific reporting routes; do not pay.
4. For large-scale attacks, document everything (screenshots, dates) and use Google's support channels.

Google removes reviews that violate policy, not reviews that are merely negative or that you disagree with. Public responses remain your main tool for genuine but unfair-feeling reviews.

### What not to do

- Threaten legal action in a public reply.
- Post fake positive reviews to "balance out" negatives.
- Ask friends to report a genuine negative review.
- Offer refunds conditional on removing a review — this is review suppression and may breach consumer law.

### Responding at scale (multi-location)

- Assign an owner per location or a central team with local input.
- Build a response style guide with tone, escalation rules and privacy rules.
- Use a review management platform or GBP's interface; avoid fully automated generic replies — personalise at least the first sentence.
- Escalate serious complaints (safety, discrimination, legal) to management immediately.

### AI-drafted replies: a safe workflow

AI assistants (including Gemini when a profile is connected to it, and general tools like Claude or ChatGPT) can draft replies quickly. Use them for **drafts**, with rules:

```text
Draft a reply to this Google review for [Business], signed by [Name, Role].
Rules: max 60 words; mention one specific thing the reviewer said; no promises we can't keep;
no personal, medical, financial or order details; no keywords or links; if negative, apologise
for the experience, invite them to contact [phone/email] and do not argue.
Review: """[paste review text only]"""
```

Then a person checks tone, accuracy and privacy before posting. Don't paste customers' personal data beyond the public review text into AI tools unless your organisation's agreements cover it. Replies that read identically across dozens of reviews undermine trust — vary them by genuinely responding to what each person said.

### Reporting: be precise

When you flag a review, choose the policy reason that actually applies (off-topic, conflict of interest, fake engagement, harassment, personal information, and so on) and keep evidence: booking records showing no such customer, screenshots, dates, patterns across reviewer profiles. Use the review management tool to check report status and appeal where available. Google removes reviews that violate policy, not reviews that are merely negative.

### Common mistakes

- Copy-paste responses for every review.
- Defensive replies that blame the customer.
- Disclosing personal or medical information.
- Ignoring reviews on other platforms customers use.
keyTakeaways: Respond to every review promptly, specifically and calmly; write for future readers.
Never disclose private information; take resolution offline.
Report reviews that violate policy with the right reason and appeal where available; negative is not the same as fake.
Never make offers conditional on removing reviews; fix root causes instead.

lessons.body:
### Reviews are free customer research

Every review is a customer telling you, unprompted, what mattered. Aggregated monthly, reviews show which services people praise, what frustrates them, which staff behaviours delight, and which locations lag. That feeds operations (fix the causes), marketing (use the language customers use) and local SEO (reviews that naturally mention services reinforce relevance).

### Step 1: Export or collect reviews

Options depend on your setup: copy recent reviews manually for a single location; use a review management platform's export; or, for developers with approved access, the Google Business Profile APIs. Keep only what you need — review text, rating, date, location — and follow your privacy notice.

### Step 2: Theme reviews with a simple, transparent method

Start with a keyword-based theme dictionary you can explain to anyone. In Google Sheets, with review text in column B:

```text
Theme: waiting   =IF(REGEXMATCH(LOWER(B2), "wait|queue|late|delay|slow"), 1, 0)
Theme: staff     =IF(REGEXMATCH(LOWER(B2), "friendly|rude|helpful|staff|team"), 1, 0)
Theme: price     =IF(REGEXMATCH(LOWER(B2), "price|expensive|cheap|value|cost"), 1, 0)
Theme: parking   =IF(REGEXMATCH(LOWER(B2), "parking|park"), 1, 0)
```

Summarise per theme and rating band with `COUNTIFS`, for example negative waiting mentions: `=COUNTIFS(Themes!C:C, 1, Reviews!C:C, "<=3")`. Add Arabic and Urdu keywords where your customers review in those languages (for example `انتظار` for waiting in Arabic).

### Step 3: Python for larger volumes

```python
import re
import pandas as pd

THEMES = {
    "waiting": r"wait|queue|late|delay|slow",
    "staff": r"friendly|rude|helpful|staff|team",
    "price": r"price|expensive|cheap|value|cost",
    "cleanliness": r"clean|dirty|hygien",
}

df = pd.read_csv("reviews.csv", parse_dates=["date"])   # columns: location,date,rating,text
df["text_l"] = df["text"].fillna("").str.lower()
for theme, pattern in THEMES.items():
    df[theme] = df["text_l"].str.contains(pattern, regex=True)

df["month"] = df["date"].dt.to_period("M")
df["negative"] = df["rating"] <= 3
summary = (df.melt(id_vars=["location", "month", "negative"], value_vars=list(THEMES),
                   var_name="theme", value_name="mentioned")
             .query("mentioned")
             .groupby(["location", "month", "theme", "negative"])
             .size().unstack("negative", fill_value=0)
             .rename(columns={False: "positive_mentions", True: "negative_mentions"}))
print(summary.tail(20))
summary.to_csv("review_themes_by_month.csv")
```

### Step 4: Optional LLM classification — with checks

Keyword themes miss nuance ("didn't have to wait at all" matches *wait*). An LLM can classify each review into your fixed theme list with sentiment. If you use one, keep the theme list fixed, ask for JSON output, send only the review text, spot-check a sample every month, and never let the model's output trigger customer-facing actions automatically. Keyword and LLM results can run side by side; where they disagree is where you learn most.

### Step 5: Turn insights into operations

| Insight | Owner | Action | Measure |
|---|---|---|---|
| Negative "waiting" mentions rising at Branch 2 on weekends | Branch manager | Add weekend staff / booking slots | Negative waiting mentions next 2 months |
| Customers praise "same-day repair" | Marketing | Add as a service + feature in posts and website | Clicks on service page; review mentions |
| Parking confusion | Operations + web | Parking photos, attribute, FAQ | Parking complaints; AI answer accuracy |

### Step 6: Feed insights back into local SEO and marketing

Reviews are also a source of **customer language**. The phrases people use ("explained everything", "same-day repair", "great with kids", "female doctor available") are often the words other customers search with and the facts AI answers repeat. Use them — honestly — in:

- **Service names and descriptions** on the profile and website, when they describe something you genuinely offer.
- **FAQs** that answer the questions behind recurring complaints (parking, waiting times, pricing clarity).
- **Posts and photos** that show what customers praise (a photo of the children's treatment room, the express lane).
- **Staff training**, using anonymised positive reviews as examples of what "great" looks like.

Never copy review text into your own marketing in a way that misrepresents it, never edit what a customer said, and follow advertising rules if you quote reviews in ads (quote accurately and don't cherry-pick in a misleading way).

### A monthly review-insights routine (30 minutes)

```text
1. Refresh the review export and re-run the theme formulas or script (5 min)
2. Compare this month's theme counts with the 3-month average per location (5 min)
3. Pick the top negative theme and top positive theme per location (5 min)
4. Update the insight → owner → action → measure table (10 min)
5. Share a 3-line summary with branch managers (5 min)
```

### Worked example (illustrative)

A three-branch car service centre in Sharjah themes 14 months of reviews. Branch B's negative "waiting" mentions double on Thursdays and Fridays; Branch A's reviews often praise "clear explanation of costs". The owner adds a booking-only express lane at Branch B on busy days, trains Branch B's advisors on Branch A's cost-explanation routine, and turns "we explain every cost before we start" into a service description and a post. Two months later Branch B's negative waiting mentions fall, and the phrase "explained everything" begins appearing in its reviews.

### Common mistakes

- Reading reviews one at a time and never aggregating.
- Treating keyword counts as precise sentiment analysis.
- Sending customer personal data to AI tools unnecessarily.
- Collecting insights without assigning owners and measures.

lessons.title: Suspensions, restrictions, appeals and fighting local spam
lessons.body:
### Three kinds of enforcement

Google Business Profile enforcement ranges from light to severe:

| Type | What happens | Typical triggers |
|---|---|---|
| **Content removal** | A review, photo, post or edit is removed or rejected | Policy-violating content |
| **Restrictions** | Limits on the profile: for fake engagement, for example, a period of not receiving new reviews, unpublished reviews, and a warning shown to customers | Fake or incentivised reviews, review gating |
| **Suspension** | The profile is disabled or stops appearing on Maps and Search, or you lose the ability to manage it | Ineligible business or address, keyword-stuffed name, suspicious ownership changes, repeated violations — sometimes in error |

Profiles also get caught by automated checks after **sensitive edits** (name, address, category) or ownership changes, which can trigger re-verification.

### Prevention: the boring habits that save you

- Keep name, address and category consistent with reality and signage; avoid frequent edits to core details.
- One profile per real location; no virtual offices or unstaffed addresses.
- Keep primary ownership on a business-controlled account with MFA; remove leavers promptly.
- Run a compliant review process (no incentives, gating, staff-name requests or kiosks).
- Keep the **evidence folder** from the setup lesson current: licence, utility bill, lease, signage and interior photos.
- Before a rebrand or move, plan the change: update signage first, then the profile, then citations and the website.

### Appeals: how to do it properly

Google provides an appeals tool for Business Profile decisions. The process, per Google's help pages:

1. Sign in with the account that manages the profile and open the **Business Profile appeals tool**.
2. Select the profile and the decision you want to appeal, and submit.
3. You'll be prompted to add **evidence via a linked form** — and Google says it must be submitted within a limited window (60 minutes at the time of writing). Have your evidence ready *before* you start.
4. Make sure business name and address on every document match the profile.
5. Wait for an email decision. If the appeal is denied, Google may allow an additional review with evidence you did not include originally.

**Evidence that tends to help:** business registration or trade licence; a utility bill or lease at the address; photos of permanent signage and the storefront in context (street, neighbouring shops); photos inside showing equipment or stock; for SABs, branded vehicles and tools. Fix any actual violation (for example remove keywords from the name) **before** appealing.

Do not create a new profile to "get around" a suspension — duplicates make things worse.

### Fighting local spam fairly

Competitors sometimes gain visibility with keyword-stuffed names, fake addresses, duplicate listings or fake reviews. You can:

- **Suggest an edit** on the competitor's profile (for example the correct name as shown on their signage), with evidence.
- **Report policy-violating reviews** you can evidence (for example, a wave of fake 5-star reviews from accounts with suspicious patterns).
- Use Google's **Business Redressal Complaint Form** for serious or repeated misrepresentation, with screenshots, signage photos and links.

Keep it factual and proportionate. Never post fake negative reviews about competitors (a conflict of interest and potentially unlawful), and don't spend more time reporting others than improving your own profile.

### Hands-on: a spam evidence log

```text
Date | Competitor | Profile URL | Issue (name/address/duplicate/reviews) | Evidence (photo/link)
Action taken (edit/report/redressal) | Reference/outcome | Re-check date
```

Photograph real-world signage (from public places) and screenshot the profile on the same day. Re-check monthly; persistent issues with good evidence are more likely to be resolved.

### Worked example (illustrative)

A locksmith in Birmingham loses pack visibility to three "locksmith" listings with keyword names like "24/7 Emergency Locksmith Birmingham Cheap" and addresses that turn out to be a parcel locker and a car park. The owner documents each (photos of the locations, screenshots, dates), suggests edits where appropriate and submits a redressal complaint for the network with all the evidence. Meanwhile he keeps working on his own profile: accurate categories, services, real photos and a steady review process. Over the following weeks some of the fake listings disappear; his visibility improves, and he keeps the log for the next time.

### Common mistakes

- Appealing without first fixing the violation.
- Starting the appeal before evidence is ready.
- Creating a new profile after a suspension.
- Retaliating with fake reviews or mass false reports.
keyTakeaways: Enforcement ranges from content removal to restrictions (for example on reviews) to suspension.
Prevent problems with accurate core details, business-owned access, compliant reviews and an up-to-date evidence folder.
Appeal through the Business Profile appeals tool, fix violations first, and have matching evidence ready before you start.
Fight competitor spam with factual edits, precise review reports and the redressal form — never with fake reviews.

lessons.title: Citations and NAP consistency
lessons.body:
### What citations are

A **citation** is any online mention of your business's **Name, Address and Phone number (NAP)**, often with the website. Citations appear in directories (Yelp, Apple Maps, Bing Places), industry sites, social profiles, local chambers, news articles and data aggregators.

Citations matter because they:

- Help search engines **corroborate** that your business exists at that location.
- Contribute to **prominence** ("information from across the web").
- Put your business where customers search (directories, apps, maps, voice assistants).
- Feed other platforms: Apple Maps, Bing Places and others supply data to assistants and car systems.

Their ranking influence is generally considered smaller than it was years ago — consistency and presence on the key platforms matter more than hundreds of low-quality listings.

### NAP consistency

Inconsistent information confuses search engines and customers. Common inconsistencies:

- Old addresses after a move.
- Different phone numbers (old line, tracking numbers, personal mobiles).
- Name variations ("Al Noor Dental", "Al-Noor Dental Clinic LLC", "AlNoor Dental").
- Suite or unit formatting ("Office 204" vs "#204") — minor; don't panic about formatting differences, but fix substantive ones.
- Duplicate listings on the same platform.

**Define your canonical NAP** and use it everywhere:

```text
Name:    Al Noor Dental Clinic
Address: Office 204, Example Tower, Al Wasl Road, Jumeirah 1, Dubai, UAE
Phone:   +971 4 000 0000
Website: https://www.alnoordental.example/
Hours:   Mon–Thu, Sat–Sun 09:00–21:00; Fri 14:00–21:00
```

Put this in a shared document and use it for every listing.

### The core citation list

Prioritise quality over quantity:

**Tier 1 — platforms that feed maps and assistants**
- Google Business Profile
- Apple Business Connect (Apple Maps)
- Bing Places for Business (can import from GBP)
- Facebook business page
- Major data aggregators relevant to your country (in the US, key aggregators feed many directories; research the current providers for your market)

**Tier 2 — major directories and review platforms relevant to your market**
- Yelp (strong in the US; present in UK and some other markets)
- Tripadvisor (hospitality)
- Trustpilot (many sectors)
- Country-specific directories (business directories, Yellow Pages equivalents, chambers of commerce)

**Tier 3 — industry and local niche sites**
- Professional bodies and associations (law societies, medical councils, trade associations)
- Industry directories (wedding, healthcare, home services, B2B)
- Local community sites, city portals, business improvement districts

Research what actually ranks for your key queries: directories that appear in organic results for "[service] [city]" are worth being listed on, because customers find them there.

### Running a citation audit

1. **Search** for your business name, variants, old names, phone numbers and old addresses.
2. **Use a citation tool** (several local SEO platforms scan major directories) to find listings and inconsistencies.
3. **Record** each listing: platform, URL, NAP shown, issues, login access.
4. **Fix** priority listings first: claim, update, merge or remove duplicates.
5. **Build** missing Tier 1 and relevant Tier 2/3 listings using the canonical NAP.
6. **Monitor** twice a year and after any change (move, rebrand, new phone).

### After a move or rebrand

- Update GBP first (address change may require re-verification).
- Update Apple, Bing, Facebook, aggregators.
- Update top directories and industry sites.
- Update the website footer, contact page and structured data.
- Search for the old address and phone periodically to catch stragglers.

### Call tracking numbers

Call tracking is useful for measurement but can create NAP inconsistency. Best practice on GBP: use the tracking number as the primary phone and the main business number as an additional phone, and use your main number on directories and the website (or dynamic number insertion for website visitors). Be consistent in your approach.

### Why citations matter more for assistants than for rankings

Map apps, in-car systems and AI assistants do not all read Google Business Profile. Apple Maps (and Siri) rely on Apple's data, which businesses manage through **Apple Business Connect**; Bing's local results — which also inform Microsoft Copilot — use **Bing Places**; and answer engines that search the web see directories, review sites and your own pages. Consistent core data across these sources is what lets any system say, confidently, "open until 10pm, on Al Wasl Road, here's the number".

### Hands-on: a citation audit sheet with formulas

Columns: `A Platform | B URL | C Name shown | D Address shown | E Phone shown | F Website shown | G Claimed? | H Notes`. Put the canonical NAP in a `Canonical` tab (B1 name, B2 address, B3 phone, B4 website). Then:

```text
Phone digits (I2):   =REGEXREPLACE(E2, "[^0-9]", "")
Phone match (J2):    =IF(RIGHT(I2, 9) = RIGHT(REGEXREPLACE(Canonical!$B$3, "[^0-9]", ""), 9), "ok", "CHECK")
Name match (K2):     =IF(LOWER(TRIM(C2)) = LOWER(TRIM(Canonical!$B$1)), "ok", "CHECK")
Website match (L2):  =IF(REGEXMATCH(LOWER(F2), REGEXREPLACE(LOWER(Canonical!$B$4), "^https?://(www\.)?", "")), "ok", "CHECK")
Issues (M2):         =COUNTIF(J2:L2, "CHECK")
```

Comparing the last nine digits of the phone number ignores country-code and formatting differences (`+971 4…`, `04…`). Address matching is best done by eye — formatting varies legitimately — so use the formulas to find substantive problems quickly and review the rest manually. Sort by `M` descending and fix Tier 1 platforms first.

### Common mistakes

- Paying for hundreds of low-quality directory submissions.
- Leaving old addresses live after moving.
- Creating duplicate listings instead of claiming existing ones.
- Different people creating listings with different name formats.
keyTakeaways: Citations are online mentions of your NAP; they corroborate existence and support prominence.
Define a canonical NAP and use it everywhere; fix substantive inconsistencies and duplicates.
Prioritise platforms that feed maps and assistants, major relevant directories and industry sites.
Audit and monitor citations, especially after moves, rebrands or phone changes.

lessons.title: Local landing pages that aren't doorways
lessons.body:
### Why local pages exist

Your website supports local visibility in two ways: it reinforces relevance for your Business Profile (Google looks at your website as part of relevance and prominence), and it can rank in organic results for local queries. **Local landing pages** — location pages for each branch, or service-in-area pages — are the main tools.

### The doorway page trap

Google's spam policies define **doorway abuse** as creating sites or pages to rank for specific, similar search queries that lead users to intermediate pages that are not as useful as the final destination. Classic examples:

- Hundreds of "[service] in [town]" pages with identical text except the town name.
- Pages for areas the business does not meaningfully serve.
- Pages that only exist to funnel users to a single contact page.

These pages often fail to rank, and at scale they can harm how Google views the site (and fall under scaled content abuse if mass-produced).

### Two legitimate page types

**1. Location pages (for real branches)**

One page per physical location, linked from the GBP profile for that location. Include:

- Exact NAP, map embed, directions and parking/transport notes.
- Opening hours (including special hours).
- Services offered at *that* location, team members, photos of *that* location.
- Reviews or testimonials from that location's customers (genuine; review markup only where eligible).
- Local details: nearby landmarks, areas served from this branch, accessibility.
- Unique content: this is a page about a real place.
- `LocalBusiness` schema with the location's details.

**2. Service-area pages (for areas genuinely served)**

For SABs or businesses serving multiple towns, create pages only where you can provide **genuinely area-specific value**:

- Projects completed in that area (case studies, photos, with client permission).
- Area-specific considerations (e.g. "Older terraced houses in Salford often have...", "In Dubai's older villa communities, AC systems commonly...").
- Local pricing or response times if they differ.
- Testimonials from customers in that area.
- Local team or depot information.

If you cannot write something meaningfully different about an area, you probably should not have a separate page for it; list it on a "Areas we serve" page instead.

### A location page template

```text
H1: Al Noor Dental Clinic — Jumeirah, Dubai
Intro: 2–3 sentences about this clinic, its team and specialisms
Key info block: address, phone, hours, directions button, parking notes
Services at this clinic: list linking to service pages
Meet the team: dentists at this location with short bios
Photos: reception, treatment rooms, exterior signage
Patient reviews: selected genuine reviews
Getting here: landmarks, metro/bus, parking
FAQs specific to this location (insurance accepted, languages spoken: Arabic, English, Urdu)
Map embed
Schema: Dentist (LocalBusiness subtype) with address, geo, hours, telephone
```

### Internal linking and store locators

- A **store locator** or locations index should link to every location page with crawlable links (not only a JavaScript map that search engines cannot navigate).
- Link location pages to relevant service pages and vice versa.
- Include the locations index in the main navigation or footer.

### Language and localisation

For bilingual markets, consider separate language versions of location pages (e.g. English and Arabic), implemented with hreflang (see the Technical SEO course). Use local phrasing and landmarks people actually use.

### Measuring local pages

Track organic impressions and clicks per location page in Search Console, GBP-linked traffic via UTMs, calls and direction requests, and conversions. Pages that attract no impressions over months may be too thin or unnecessary.

### Illustrative example

A home-cleaning company in London had 120 near-identical "cleaners in [borough]" pages. It consolidated them into 12 area hub pages for zones it genuinely serves, each with team information, customer stories and area-specific advice, and redirected the thin pages to the relevant hub. The consolidated pages were easier to maintain and more useful to visitors. (Illustrative scenario; outcomes vary.)

### Hands-on: catch city-swap pages with a similarity check

Before publishing (or when auditing) a set of location or service-area pages, measure how similar they are. This Python script compares the visible text of each pair of pages using word shingles and flags pairs that are nearly identical:

```python
import itertools
import re
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

URLS = [
    "https://www.example.com/areas/salford/",
    "https://www.example.com/areas/stockport/",
    "https://www.example.com/areas/trafford/",
]

def text(url: str) -> str:
    r = requests.get(url, timeout=15, headers={"User-Agent": "page-similarity/1.0"})
    r.raise_for_status()
    soup = BeautifulSoup(r.text, "html.parser")
    for t in soup(["script", "style", "nav", "header", "footer"]):
        t.decompose()
    return " ".join(soup.get_text(" ").lower().split())

def shingles(s: str, k: int = 5) -> set:
    words = re.findall(r"\w+", s)
    return {" ".join(words[i:i + k]) for i in range(max(len(words) - k + 1, 1))}

pages = {u: shingles(text(u)) for u in URLS}
for a, b in itertools.combinations(URLS, 2):
    inter, union = len(pages[a] & pages[b]), len(pages[a] | pages[b]) or 1
    sim = inter / union
    flag = "  <-- likely city-swap" if sim > 0.6 else ""
    print(f"{sim:.2f}  {a}  vs  {b}{flag}")
```

A high similarity score is not a Google metric, and there is no official threshold — it is a prompt to ask: *what on this page is genuinely about this place?* If the honest answer is "only the town name", consolidate.

### AI-assisted drafting without doorways

AI tools can help draft location pages from a structured brief, but only from **real, location-specific inputs**: the branch's team, services actually offered there, photos taken there, directions, local projects with permission, and reviews from that branch's customers. Generating hundreds of area pages from a template and a town list is exactly the pattern Google's scaled content abuse and doorway policies describe. For page systems at scale, see **Programmatic SEO and AI Content at Scale (programmatic-seo-and-ai-content-at-scale)**.

### Common mistakes

- City-swap template pages.
- Location pages without real local content or photos.
- Store locators that search engines cannot crawl.
- Linking all GBP profiles to the home page instead of the location page (for multi-location businesses).
keyTakeaways: Doorway abuse includes near-identical city-swap pages created only to rank.
Build location pages for real branches with unique, useful details and LocalBusiness schema.
Create service-area pages only where you can add genuinely area-specific value; otherwise use one 'areas served' page.
Make location pages reachable via crawlable store locators and link each GBP profile to its location page.
